originalTitle: Warren Buffett Says His Favorite Holding Period Is Forever. A Secretary Who Paid $180 for 3 Shares in 1935 and Never Sold Died Worth $7 Million. Here’s What Her Rule Does for $600,000 in One Stock Today
summary: Warren Buffett's favorite holding period is forever. Grace Groner, a secretary at Abbott, paid $180 for three shares in 1935, reinvested every dividend, never sold, and left Lake Forest College $7 million when she died at 100 in 2010. Here is what the splits did, what the dividends did, what the S&P 500 would have paid, the fall she sat through at 93, and what her rule does for a retired couple holding $600,000 of one old stock today.

Warren Buffett wrote in his 1988 letter to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders that "when we own portions of outstanding businesses with outstanding managements, our favorite holding period is forever." The best proof of that rule was a secretary in Lake Forest, Illinois, named Grace Groner. In 1935 she paid $180 for three shares of Abbott Laboratories, the company that employed her. She never sold a share and reinvested every dividend. When she died in January 2010 at 100, her estate came to $7 million, and she left it all to Lake Forest College, her alma mater, through a foundation she had set up for the purpose.

The Chicago Tribune told her story in March 2010: 43 years as a secretary at Abbott, a one-bedroom cottage that had been willed to her, clothes from rummage sales, no car. "Oh, my God," the college’s president, Stephen Schutt, said when he learned the amount. About 1,300 students have since taken internships and study abroad on her money.

Her $7 million reads as the strongest case anyone has made for Buffett’s rule that the best holding period is forever, and the limit of that reading is that she held one company that kept raising its dividend for 54 straight years, so the rule only did its work because the company did. Here is what her $180 became, where the money came from, what the same rule costs, and what it would do for a reader holding one old stock today.

What $180 Became, and Where It Came From

Three shares at $60 in 1935, $7 million in January 2010: that is a multiple of 38,889 times over 75 years, or 15.1% a year compounded. The same $180 in the S&P 500 with every dividend reinvested, from the start of 1935 through the end of 2009, would have grown to about $341,282, by Damodaran’s annual return series at NYU Stern, which is 10.6% a year. She beat the index 21 times over.

The part most retellings skip is where the money came from. Abbott’s own investor site lists eight stock splits since she bought in, one 3-for-1 in 1964 and seven 2-for-1 splits between 1975 and 1998, a factor of 384. Splits alone would have turned her three shares into 1,152 shares. At Abbott’s $53.99 close on December 31, 2009, those were worth $62,196. Price appreciation by itself gave her 346 times her money, or 8.1% a year.

Everything else, 99.1% of the estate, came from the dividends she reinvested, and from the dividends those new shares paid in turn. At $53.99 a share, $7 million is about 129,654 shares, 113 times what the splits alone would have left her. The dividend, reinvested without a break for 75 years, was the engine. The stock price was the fuel.

Her $180 in 1935 is about $4,426 in today’s dollars, by the consumer price index. Leave $4,400 alone for 40 years at the index’s 10.6% and it becomes about $246,396.

Groner and her twin sister were born on a farm in Lake County in 1909 and orphaned at 12. A local family, the Andersons, took them in and paid for Lake Forest College, where both graduated in 1931. She went to work at Abbott the same year and bought her shares four years later. The foundation’s own page says she "lived humbly and kept her wealth a secret." She gave $180,000 to help start a scholarship fund at the college while she was alive and went to its football games. Her longtime friend and lawyer, William Marlatt, told the Tribune that "she did not have the (material) needs that other people have." The $7 million works out to $162,791 for every year she worked at Abbott. She never earned anything like that. Her shares did.

Abbott has paid 410 consecutive quarterly dividends since 1924 and has raised its payout for 54 straight years. Its current dividend is $2.52 a year, $0.63 a quarter, a 6.8% raise over last year, which at Wednesday’s close of $109.29 is a 2.3% yield. On the 129,654 shares her estate held in 2010, today’s dividend would be about $326,727 a year. The stock has doubled since the end of 2009.

That record is the reason her rule worked, and it is also why the rule is dangerous in the wrong hands. Every company that paid a dividend in 1935 looked solid to the secretary who typed its letters, and many of them are gone. Even Abbott, on month-end prices with dividends reinvested, fell 36.8% between January 2002 and February 2003. She was 93 that year, with everything she owned in one stock. She did nothing, and that was the right call for her, because she had a pension and Social Security and no plan to spend the shares.

What Her Rule Does for a Reader’s Dollars Today

Take a retired engineer, 67, and his wife, 66, with $2.4 million, who did a smaller version of what she did: $60,000 of one dividend stock bought through an employee plan in the 1990s, now worth $600,000, 25% of everything they own, paying $13,800 a year. He draws $70,000 a year from his IRA and the couple collects $40,800 in Social Security. The stock is their only concentrated position, and the question that comes up every December is whether to sell it. If you hold something like it, the numbers below are yours too.

Groner’s rule says hold, and the tax code agrees with her more than most holders realize. Selling the whole position this year realizes a $540,000 long-term gain and lifts their adjusted gross income from $118,480 to $658,480. The $12,000 senior deduction they get as a couple over 65 phases out completely. The gain stacks on top of their ordinary income, most of it at 15% and the last $9,280 at 20% above the $613,700 line, for $79,076 of capital gains tax. The 3.8% net investment income tax, which starts at $250,000 of income for a couple, adds $15,522. 这篇文章可能包含来自我们的赞助商和附属机构的链接，Flywheel Publishing 可能会因通过他们采取的行动而获得补偿。

沃伦·巴菲特在 1988 年写给伯克希尔·哈撒韦公司股东的信中写道：“当我们拥有部分优秀企业和优秀管理层时，我们最喜欢的持有期是永远。”这条规则的最好证明是伊利诺伊州森林湖的一位名叫格蕾丝·格罗纳的秘书。 1935 年，她以 180 美元购买了雇用她的雅培公司 (Abbott Laboratories) 的三股股票。她从未出售过股票，并将所有股息都进行了再投资。 2010 年 1 月，100 岁的她去世时，她的遗产达到了 700 万美元，她通过为此目的设立的基金会将其全部留给了母校森林湖学院。

《芝加哥论坛报》在 2010 年 3 月讲述了她的故事：在雅培公司担任秘书 43 年，她遗嘱里有一套单卧室小屋，衣服是从旧货中淘来的，没有汽车。 “哦，天啊，”学院院长史蒂芬·舒特（Stephen Schutt）得知这个数字后说道。此后，约有 1,300 名学生用她的钱去实习和出国留学。

她的 700 万美元被解读为巴菲特“最佳持有期是永远”这一规则的最强有力的论证，而这一解读的局限性在于，她持有一家连续 54 年不断提高股息的公司，所以这条规则之所以起作用，是因为该公司这样做了。以下是她的 180 美元变成了什么、钱从哪里来、同样的规则的成本是多少，以及对于今天持有一只旧股票的读者来说会产生什么影响。

180 美元变成了什么，它从何而来

1935 年 3 股价格为 60 美元，2010 年 1 月为 700 万美元：这是 75 年中 38,889 倍的倍数，即每年复利 15.1%。从 1935 年初到 2009 年底，标准普尔 500 指数中每笔股息再投资的 180 美元，根据达莫达兰在纽约大学斯特恩商学院的年回报率系列计算，每年回报率为 10.6%，将增长到约 341,282 美元。她跑赢了该指数 21 倍。

大多数重述都跳过的部分是钱的来源。雅培自己的投资者网站列出了自她买入以来的 8 次股票分割，其中 1964 年进行了 1 次 3 换 1，1975 年至 1998 年间进行了 7 次 2 换 1，比例为 384。仅通过分割就可以将她的 3 股变成 1,152 股。以雅培 2009 年 12 月 31 日收盘价 53.99 美元计算，这些股票的价值为 62,196 美元。价格上涨本身就给她带来了 346 倍的收入，即每年 8.1%。

其他的一切，即99.1%的遗产，都来自她再投资的股息，以及这些新股依次支付的股息。以每股 53.99 美元计算，700 万美元相当于 129,654 股，是仅拆分后她所剩资产的 113 倍。 75年来不间断地进行再投资的股息是引擎。股票价格是燃料。

根据消费者价格指数，她 1935 年的收入为 180 美元，换算成今天的美元约为 4,426 美元。如果 4,400 美元在该指数 10.6% 的情况下保持 40 年，则其价值约为 246,396 美元。

格罗纳和她的双胞胎姐妹 1909 年出生在莱克县的一个农场，12 岁时成为孤儿。当地的安德森家族收养了她们，并出资入读了森林湖学院，两人均于 1931 年毕业。同年，格罗纳到雅培工作，四年后购买了自己的股票。该基金会自己的页面称，她“生活谦虚，对自己的财富保密”。她在世时捐赠了 18 万美元，帮助学院设立奖学金基金，并观看了学院的橄榄球比赛。她的老朋友兼律师威廉·马拉特告诉《论坛报》，“她没有其他人有的（物质）需求。”她在 Abbott 工作的每年 700 万美元相当于 162,791 美元。她从来没有赚过这样的钱。她的股票确实如此。

自 1924 年以来，雅培已连续支付 410 次季度股息，并连续 54 年提高派息。目前的股息为每年 2.52 美元，每季度 0.63 美元，比去年增加 6.8%，周三收盘价为 109.29 美元，收益率为 2.3%。按照她 2010 年持有的 129,654 股遗产计算，今天的股息每年约为 326,727 美元。自2009年底以来，该股已翻倍。

这一记录是她的规则发挥作用的原因，也是为什么该规则落入坏人之手是危险的。每家 1935 年派发股息的公司在打下信件的秘书看来都十分稳固，但其中许多都已经消失了。就连雅培公司（按股息再投资的月末价格计算），在 2002 年 1 月至 2003 年 2 月期间也下跌了 36.8%。那一年她已经 93 岁了，她所拥有的一切都集中在一只股票上。她什么也没做，这对她来说是正确的选择，因为她有养老金和社会保障，而且没有计划花掉股票。

她的规则对今天读者的钱有什么影响

以一位 67 岁的退休工程师和他 66 岁的妻子为例，他们拥有 240 万美元，他们做了一个较小的版本：通过 20 世纪 90 年代的员工计划购买了 60,000 美元的股息股票，现在价值 600,000 美元，占他们拥有的一切的 25%，每年支付 13,800 美元。他每年从 IRA 中提取 70,000 美元，这对夫妇则领取 40,800 美元的社会保障金。该股票是他们唯一集中持有的头寸，每年 12 月都会出现的问题是是否出售该股票。如果你持有类似的东西，下面的数字也是你的。
